entries.summary: Joints are divided by the tissue joining the bones into fibrous, cartilaginous and synovial joints. Synovial joints are the most mobile and are subdivided by the shape of their articular surfaces.
facts: Synchondroses (hyaline cartilage; e.g. growth plate, 1st rib–sternum) and symphyses (fibrocartilage; e.g. pubic symphysis, intervertebral discs)
Have a joint cavity, articular cartilage, capsule, synovial membrane and synovial fluid
Plane, hinge (ginglymus – elbow), pivot (trochoid – proximal radioulnar), saddle (sellar – thumb CMC), ellipsoid (wrist), ball-and-socket (spheroidal – shoulder, hip), bicondylar (knee)
sections: Axes of movement
Uniaxial joints (hinge, pivot) move in one plane, biaxial joints (saddle, ellipsoid) in two planes and multiaxial joints (ball-and-socket) in all planes.
Hilton's law
The nerves that supply the muscles crossing a joint also supply the joint and the skin over it.
clinical: Osteoarthritis is degeneration of the articular cartilage; rheumatoid arthritis is autoimmune inflammation of the synovial membrane.
tus: Fibrous joints: suture, syndesmosis, gomphosis; cartilaginous joints: synchondrosis (hyaline), symphysis (fibrocartilage); the rest are synovial.
Types of synovial joint: plane, hinge, pivot, ellipsoid (condylar), saddle, ball-and-socket; bicondylar joints (knee, TMJ) are counted separately.

entries.summary: Freely movable joints with a fluid-filled joint cavity between the bone ends. The articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage; a fibrous capsule encloses the joint and a synovial membrane lines it.
facts: Articular cartilage (usually hyaline), joint cavity, joint capsule (fibrous membrane outside, synovial membrane inside), synovial fluid
Ligaments (extracapsular, intracapsular), discs and menisci, labra, fat pads, bursae
A slippery fluid rich in hyaluronic acid produced by the synovial membrane; it nourishes the cartilage and reduces friction
Supplied by arterial networks around the joint; by Hilton's law the nerves supplying the muscles that cross a joint also supply the joint
Articular cartilage has no vessels or nerves; it is nourished by diffusion from the synovial fluid
sections: Bursae and tendon sheaths

A bursa is a small sac lined by synovial membrane between structures that rub against each other, such as tendon and bone or skin and bone. Some communicate with the joint cavity (e.g. the suprapatellar bursa). Tendon sheaths (synovial sheaths) wrap long tendons in osteofibrous tunnels; they are prominent around the wrist and ankle.
Joint stability

The stability of a joint depends on three factors: the shape and fit of the articular surfaces (hip), the strength of the ligaments (knee) and the tone of the surrounding muscles (shoulder). Joints with a large range of movement are usually less stable.
clinical: Osteoarthritis involves wear of the articular cartilage; joint space narrowing, osteophytes and subchondral sclerosis are seen.
Rheumatoid arthritis is chronic inflammation of the synovial membrane; the pannus erodes cartilage and bone.
Bursitis (e.g. prepatellar bursitis – 'housemaid's knee', olecranon bursitis) develops with repeated pressure or friction.
tus: Hilton's law: the nerves supplying the muscles that cross a joint also supply the joint and the skin over it.
Articular cartilage is avascular and has no perichondrium; therefore its damage does not heal.

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: The synovial joint between the condylar process of the mandible and the mandibular fossa and articular tubercle of the temporal bone. A fibrocartilaginous disc divides it into upper and lower compartments.
facts: Head of the mandible – mandibular fossa and articular tubercle (temporal bone)
Fibrocartilage; gliding (translation) in the upper compartment, hinge movement (rotation) in the lower
Lateral (temporomandibular) ligament, sphenomandibular ligament, stylomandibular ligament
Opening and closing, protrusion and retrusion, side-to-side (grinding) movements
clinical: When the mouth opens too wide (yawning) the head of the mandible can slip in front of the articular tubercle and the mouth cannot close (TMJ dislocation).
TMJ disorders (disc displacement, clicking, pain) are associated with tooth grinding and stress.
tus: The TMJ is a hinge-and-glide (ginglymoarthrodial) joint; its articular surfaces are fibrocartilage.
The lateral (temporomandibular) ligament is the only true reinforcement of the capsule; the sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments are accessory.

entries.tr: Disc and ligaments of the temporomandibular joint
entries.en: Disc and ligaments of the TMJ
entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: The fibrocartilaginous disc inside the temporomandibular joint divides the joint cavity into upper and lower compartments. The joint is supported laterally by the lateral ligament and at a distance by the sphenomandibular and stylomandibular ligaments.
facts: Biconcave fibrocartilage disc; attached in front to the upper head of lateral pterygoid and behind to the bilaminar zone (retrodiscal tissue)
Upper compartment: gliding (translation); lower compartment: hinge (rotation)
From the zygomatic arch to the neck of the mandible; a thickening of the capsule that prevents the condyle from moving backwards
Sphenomandibular ligament (spine of the sphenoid – lingula of the mandible), stylomandibular ligament (styloid process – angle of the mandible), pterygospinous ligament
sections: Mechanism of mouth opening

In the first stage of opening the condyle rotates about its own axis in the lower compartment; on wider opening the condyle and disc glide together forwards in the upper compartment towards the articular tubercle. This forward glide is produced mainly by the lateral pterygoid.
clinical: In temporomandibular disorders the disc may be displaced forwards; there is a click and pain on opening, and in later stages opening locks.
In dislocation of the jaw the condyle slips in front of the articular tubercle and the mouth cannot close; it is reduced by pressing downwards and backwards.
tus: The muscle that pulls the disc forwards is the lateral pterygoid; dislocation of the TMJ is always anterior.
The sphenomandibular ligament is a remnant of the 1st pharyngeal arch (Meckel's cartilage).

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: The joints between the skull and the first two cervical vertebrae: the atlanto-occipital joint between the occipital condyles and the atlas, and the atlanto-axial joints between the atlas and the axis. They allow the 'yes' (nodding) and 'no' (turning) movements of the head.
facts: Occipital condyles – superior articular facets of the atlas; ellipsoid synovial joint; flexion-extension of the head ('yes') and slight lateral bending
Median atlanto-axial joint in the middle (dens – anterior arch of atlas and transverse ligament; pivot joint), lateral atlanto-axial joints on each side (plane); rotation of the head ('no')

Cruciform ligament of the atlas (transverse ligament and longitudinal bands), alar ligaments (from the dens to the occipital condyles; limit excessive rotation), apical ligament of the dens, tectorial membrane (continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament), anterior and posterior atlanto-occipital membranes
About half of neck rotation takes place at the atlanto-axial joint and a large part of flexion-extension at the atlanto-occipital joint
sections: Transverse ligament of the atlas

The most important ligament holding the dens against the anterior arch of the atlas and preventing it from shifting backwards into the spinal cord. If it ruptures, the dens can compress the spinal cord and medulla oblongata.
clinical: In rheumatoid arthritis and Down syndrome laxity of the transverse ligament can cause atlanto-axial instability and cord compression.
Fractures of the dens (especially type II – base of the dens) are common in falls in the elderly and carry a high risk of non-union.
A burst fracture of the atlas (Jefferson fracture) results from vertical loading on the top of the head.
tus: The atlanto-occipital joint allows the 'yes' movement, the atlanto-axial joint the 'no' movement.
The alar ligaments limit excessive rotation of the head; the tectorial membrane is the continuation of the posterior longitudinal ligament up to the skull base.

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: Fibrocartilaginous cushions between adjacent vertebral bodies, with a ring-shaped annulus fibrosus outside and a jelly-like nucleus pulposus in the centre. They make up about a quarter of the length of the spine.
facts: Annulus fibrosus (concentric collagen lamellae), nucleus pulposus (notochord remnant, 80% water)
23 discs; none between C1 and C2 or in the sacrum and coccyx
Largely avascular in adults; nourished by diffusion from the end plates
sections: Changes with age
With age the nucleus pulposus loses water and the discs lose height; this underlies loss of stature and degenerative disc disease.
clinical: In disc herniation the nucleus pulposus usually tears through the annulus posterolaterally and presses on a nerve root; in the lumbar spine the L4–L5 disc affects the L5 root and the L5–S1 disc the S1 root.
In the neck the C5–C6 disc compresses the C6 root.
tus: The discs make up about 1/4 of the length of the spine; there is no disc between atlas and axis.
A cervical disc herniation compresses the root of the same number (C5–C6 → C6), a lumbar one the root below (L4–L5 → L5).

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: Ligaments that bind the vertebrae together and stabilise the spine. Long ligaments run the whole length of the spine, short ones between neighbouring vertebrae.
facts: Anterior longitudinal ligament (front of the bodies – limits hyperextension), posterior longitudinal ligament (back of the bodies, inside the vertebral canal – limits hyperflexion), supraspinous ligament, ligamentum nuchae (in the neck)
Ligamenta flava (between the laminae, yellow elastic ligament), interspinous ligaments, intertransverse ligaments
A triangular ligament from C7 to the external occipital protuberance; gives attachment to trapezius and splenius
sections: Course of the ligaments

The anterior longitudinal ligament runs on the front of the vertebral bodies from the skull base to the sacrum and prevents hyperextension. The posterior longitudinal ligament lies in the front wall of the vertebral canal, on the back of the bodies; because it narrows in the lumbar region, disc herniations are often posterolateral. The ligamenta flava are made of yellow elastic fibres, join the laminae and help the spine straighten after flexion.
clinical: In lumbar puncture the needle passes through skin, supraspinous ligament, interspinous ligament, ligamentum flavum, epidural space and dura–arachnoid; a loss of resistance is felt after the ligamentum flavum.
In ankylosing spondylitis the ligaments ossify, giving a 'bamboo spine'.
tus: The anterior longitudinal ligament limits hyperextension, the posterior one hyperflexion.
The ligamentum nuchae is the triangular continuation of the supraspinous ligament in the neck; it gives attachment to trapezius and splenius.

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: Small synovial joints between the articular processes of adjacent vertebrae (facet joints). The cervical vertebrae also have uncovertebral (Luschka) joints at the lateral margins of the bodies. The orientation of these joints determines the type of movement in each region.
facts: Facet joints: synovial plane joints; uncovertebral joints: cleft-like joints at the lateral margin of the disc

Cervical region near horizontal (inclined front to back) – movement in all directions; thoracic region in the frontal plane – rotation; lumbar region in the sagittal plane – flexion-extension, rotation limited
Medial branches of the posterior rami of the spinal nerves; each facet joint receives fibres from two adjacent levels
Between the uncinate processes on the upper lateral margins of the C3–C7 bodies and the vertebra above
clinical: Facet joint arthrosis is a common cause of back and neck pain; it can be treated by medial branch block or radiofrequency ablation.
Osteophytes of the uncovertebral joints can narrow the intervertebral foramen and cause cervical radiculopathy.
In spondylolysis there is a defect in the pars interarticularis (usually L5); on oblique X-ray it gives the 'collar on the Scottie dog' appearance.
tus: The lumbar facets lie in the sagittal plane, so rotation is limited in the lumbar region; in the thoracic region rotation is free.
The pars interarticularis is the bony bridge between the superior and inferior articular processes; its stress fracture is spondylolysis.

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: The joints of the ribs with the vertebrae (costovertebral) and with the sternum (sternocostal). They let the thoracic cage expand during breathing.
facts: Joint of the head of the rib (rib head – two neighbouring vertebral bodies) and costotransverse joint (rib tubercle – transverse process)
1st rib: synchondrosis; ribs 2–7: synovial plane joints
Interchondral joints (between cartilages 6–9), costochondral joints (rib–cartilage; hyaline cartilage union)
clinical: Costochondral separation can occur in chest trauma and is painful like a rib fracture; it may not be visible on X-ray.
tus: The upper ribs move like a pump handle (anteroposterior diameter), the lower ribs like a bucket handle (transverse diameter).
Ribs 11 and 12 have no costotransverse joint.

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: Behind, each rib forms two joints with the vertebrae: the joint of the head of the rib with the vertebral bodies and the costotransverse joint between the tubercle of the rib and the transverse process. These joints allow the ribs to move in breathing.
facts: In typical ribs the head articulates with two adjacent vertebral bodies and the disc between them; reinforced by the radiate ligament and the intra-articular ligament
Tubercle of the rib – transverse process of the vertebra of the same number; reinforced by the costotransverse, superior and lateral costotransverse ligaments (absent in the 11th and 12th ribs)
'Pump-handle' movement in the upper ribs (increases the anteroposterior diameter), 'bucket-handle' movement in the lower ribs (increases the transverse diameter)
clinical: In ankylosing spondylitis involvement of the costovertebral joints reduces chest expansion and lowers respiratory capacity.
tus: The heads of the 1st, 10th, 11th and 12th ribs articulate only with the vertebra of their own number (single facet).
The pump-handle movement increases the anteroposterior diameter of the chest in the upper ribs, the bucket-handle movement the transverse diameter in the lower ribs.
models: Radiate ligament of head of rib
Intra-articular ligament of head of rib

entries.group: Joints of the skull and spine
entries.summary: Small cartilaginous joint between the apex of the sacrum and the base of the coccyx; it is reinforced by a thin disc and ligaments.
facts: Symphysis (secondary cartilaginous joint); may ossify with age
Anterior, superficial and deep posterior and lateral sacrococcygeal ligaments; intercornual ligaments between the sacral and coccygeal cornua
During childbirth the coccyx moves slightly backwards, widening the pelvic outlet
clinical: Coccydynia (tailbone pain) usually develops after a fall in the sitting position or after childbirth, from strain of this joint.
tus: During childbirth the coccyx moves backwards, increasing the anteroposterior diameter of the pelvic outlet.

entries.summary: The joint between the medial end of the clavicle and the manubrium and 1st costal cartilage. It is the only true joint between the upper limb and the trunk.
facts: Synovial saddle joint (functionally ball-and-socket); contains an articular disc
Anterior and posterior sternoclavicular ligaments, interclavicular ligament, costoclavicular ligament (the strongest)
Elevation–depression, protraction–retraction and rotation of the clavicle
sections: Structure and stability

The medial end of the clavicle articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the 1st costal cartilage. The articular surfaces are incongruent; the articular disc divides the cavity into two and prevents the clavicle from sliding medially. It is the only bony joint attaching the upper limb to the trunk; its stability comes mainly from the costoclavicular ligament.
clinical: Posterior dislocation is rare but an emergency, because it can compress the great vessels and trachea behind it.
tus: The articular disc stops the clavicle sliding medially; its strongest ligament is the costoclavicular ligament.
Posterior dislocation is rare but an emergency because it can compress the trachea and great vessels.
Posterior dislocation of the sternoclavicular joint is rare but an emergency because of the great vessels and trachea behind it.

entries.summary: A small plane joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the acromion of the scapula. Its main stability comes from the coracoclavicular ligament outside the joint.
facts: Acromioclavicular ligament; coracoclavicular ligament (trapezoid and conoid ligaments) – the main stabiliser
Gliding and rotation of the scapula on the clavicle
sections: Structure

A plane joint between the lateral end of the clavicle and the medial margin of the acromion; an incomplete disc may be present. The acromioclavicular ligament provides horizontal stability, the coracoclavicular ligaments (conoid and trapezoid) vertical stability.
clinical: A fall on the shoulder can separate the AC joint (unlike a shoulder dislocation); if the coracoclavicular ligament also tears, the end of the clavicle rises markedly (piano-key sign).
tus: A synovial plane joint; it lets the scapula rotate on the clavicle.
In Rockwood type III and higher injuries the coracoclavicular ligament is also torn.

entries.tr: Ligaments of the scapula and coraco-acromial arch
entries.summary: Ligaments stretched between parts of the scapula itself. The coraco-acromial ligament forms, with the acromion and coracoid process, a protective arch over the shoulder joint; the transverse scapular ligaments complete the openings through which the suprascapular nerve and vessels pass.
facts: Acromion, coraco-acromial ligament and coracoid process; prevents the humeral head from moving upwards; the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa lie beneath it
Converts the suprascapular notch into a foramen: the suprascapular nerve passes below it, the suprascapular artery and vein above
Between the lateral border of the spine of the scapula and the glenoid cavity; the suprascapular nerve and artery pass beneath it to the infraspinous fossa
Conoid ligament (medial, cone-shaped) and trapezoid ligament (lateral); suspend the clavicle from the scapula and provide vertical stability of the AC joint
clinical: In impingement syndrome the supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa are pinched under the coraco-acromial arch as the arm is raised sideways; the painful arc lies between 60 and 120°.
Entrapment of the suprascapular nerve at the suprascapular notch causes wasting of supraspinatus and infraspinatus; at the spinoglenoid notch (inferior ligament) only infraspinatus is affected.
tus: At the suprascapular notch the nerve passes below the ligament and the artery above it ('Army over Navy': artery above, nerve below).
AC dislocations are graded (Rockwood) according to whether the coracoclavicular ligaments are torn.

entries.summary: The ball-and-socket joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid cavity of the scapula. It is the most mobile and most frequently dislocated joint in the body; its stability depends largely on the rotator cuff muscles.
facts: Head of humerus – glenoid cavity (deepened by the glenoid labrum); only 1/3 of the head contacts the socket
Glenohumeral ligaments (superior, middle, inferior), coracohumeral ligament, transverse humeral ligament, coracoacromial ligament (roof of the joint)
Rotator cuff (SITS: supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), long head of biceps tendon, labrum
Flexion–extension, abduction–adduction, internal and external rotation, circumduction
Axillary nerve, suprascapular nerve, lateral pectoral nerve
sections: Capsule
The capsule is lax and weakest below (axillary recess); the long head of biceps tendon runs inside the capsule.
clinical: 95% of shoulder dislocations are anterior-inferior; the axillary nerve can be injured. Recurrent dislocations cause a tear of the anterior-inferior labrum (Bankart lesion) and a dent in the posterolateral humeral head (Hill–Sachs lesion).
In frozen shoulder (adhesive capsulitis) the capsule thickens and contracts, limiting movement in all directions.
SLAP lesion: tear of the superior labrum at the attachment of the biceps tendon.
tus: The stability of the glenohumeral joint depends more on the rotator cuff muscles than on bone.
Anterior dislocation causes a Hill–Sachs lesion (notch in the posterosuperior humeral head) and a Bankart lesion (anterior-inferior labral tear).

entries.tr: Ligaments and labrum of the shoulder joint
entries.summary: The three glenohumeral ligaments on the front of the shoulder capsule, the coracohumeral ligament above and the fibrocartilaginous labrum deepening the rim of the glenoid cavity are the passive stabilisers of the joint.
facts: Fibrocartilaginous ring attached to the rim of the glenoid cavity; deepens the socket by about 50%; the long head of biceps arises from its upper part
Superior, middle and inferior on the front of the capsule; the inferior is the most important and protects against anterior dislocation with the arm in abduction and external rotation
From the coracoid process to the greater and lesser tubercles; reinforces the rotator interval and prevents the arm from slipping downwards
Bridges the intertubercular groove between the greater and lesser tubercles, holding the tendon of the long head of biceps in its groove
The lower part of the capsule (axillary recess) and the rotator interval between subscapularis and supraspinatus
clinical: A Bankart lesion is a tear of the anteroinferior labrum and inferior glenohumeral ligament; it is the main cause of recurrent anterior dislocations.
If the transverse humeral ligament tears, the long head of biceps tendon can slip out of its groove (subluxation) and cause a painful click.
A SLAP lesion is a tear of the superior labrum from front to back; it occurs in throwing sports.
tus: The inferior glenohumeral ligament is the most important static stabiliser against anterior dislocation in abduction and external rotation.
The long head of biceps arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and superior labrum; it runs inside the capsule within a synovial sheath.

entries.summary: A compound joint between the humerus, ulna and radius inside a single capsule, made up of the humeroulnar, humeroradial and proximal radioulnar joints.
facts: Compound synovial joint: humeroulnar (hinge), humeroradial (ball-and-socket), proximal radioulnar (pivot)
Ulnar collateral ligament (medial), radial collateral ligament (lateral), annular ligament (ring around the radial head)
Flexion–extension (0–145°); pronation–supination at the proximal radioulnar joint
A 10–15° outward angle between arm and forearm in extension (greater in women)
sections: Cubital fossa
In the triangular hollow in front of the elbow lie, from lateral to medial, the biceps tendon, brachial artery and median nerve. The superficial median cubital vein is used for blood sampling.
clinical: Elbow dislocation is usually posterior.
Lateral epicondylitis (tennis elbow) and medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow) are overuse injuries of the tendon origins.
In children the radial head can slip out of the annular ligament ('pulled elbow').
tus: Elbow dislocations are usually posterolateral; disruption of the triangle (olecranon and epicondyles) distinguishes dislocation from fracture.
In extension the olecranon and epicondyles lie in a straight line; in flexion they form a triangle (Hueter's triangle).

entries.summary: The elbow joint is supported on each side by collateral ligaments, and the head of the radius by the ring-shaped annular ligament. The proximal radio-ulnar joint is also strengthened by the quadrate ligament and the oblique cord.
facts: From the medial epicondyle to the coronoid process and olecranon; triangular, with anterior, posterior and transverse (oblique) bands; resists valgus force – its most important part is the anterior band
From the lateral epicondyle, blending with the annular ligament; resists varus force
Attached to the front and back margins of the radial notch of the ulna; encircles 4/5 of the circumference of the radial head
Between the neck of the radius and the lower margin of the radial notch; limits excessive supination and pronation
Thin band running down and laterally from the ulnar tuberosity to the radius; its fibres run opposite to those of the interosseous membrane
clinical: In baseball pitchers and javelin throwers repeated valgus stress tears the anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament; its reconstruction with a tendon graft is known as 'Tommy John' surgery.
In pulled elbow (subluxation of the radial head) the radial head slips under the annular ligament; it is reduced by supination and flexion.
tus: The anterior band of the ulnar collateral ligament is the most important structure for valgus stability of the elbow; the ulnar nerve passes just behind this ligament.
The inner surface of the annular ligament is lined with cartilage and works like an articular surface with the radial head.

entries.summary: The two synovial joints between the upper and lower ends of the radius and ulna, together with the interosseous membrane between their shafts. Together they produce pronation and supination of the forearm.
facts: Pivot joint; the radial head turns in the radial notch of the ulna within the annular ligament
Pivot joint; head of ulna – ulnar notch of the radius; reinforced by the articular disc (part of the TFCC)
Its fibres run downwards and medially from radius to ulna; they transfer force from the hand and radius to the ulna
Pronation (pronator teres, pronator quadratus) and supination (supinator, biceps brachii); about 150° in total
clinical: Tears of the triangular fibrocartilage complex (TFCC) are a common cause of ulnar-sided wrist pain.
tus: At the proximal radioulnar joint the radial head turns within the annular ligament; distally the radius turns around the ulnar head.
The fibres of the interosseous membrane run down and medially from radius to ulna and transfer load from the hand to the ulna.
The main stabiliser of the distal radio-ulnar joint is the TFCC; in a Galeazzi fracture (radial shaft) this joint dislocates, in a Monteggia fracture (ulna) the radial head dislocates.

entries.summary: A structure between the distal ulna and the carpal bones, made of an articular disc and the ligaments around it. It stabilises the distal radio-ulnar joint and carries the load on the ulnar side of the wrist.
facts: Articular disc (triangular fibrocartilage), dorsal and palmar radio-ulnar ligaments, ulnolunate and ulnotriquetral ligaments, ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist, sheath of the extensor carpi ulnaris tendon, meniscus homologue
The base of the disc attaches to the lower margin of the ulnar notch of the radius, its apex to the base of the ulnar styloid (fovea)
Main stabiliser of the distal radio-ulnar joint; carries about 20% of the load passing through the wrist; separates the ulna from the radiocarpal joint
Only its outer margin (periphery) is well vascularised; its centre is avascular
clinical: TFCC tears occur with falls on the outstretched hand or repeated rotation; they cause ulnar-sided wrist pain, clicking and weak grip.
With ulna plus variance (ulna longer than the radius) the TFCC and lunate wear (ulnocarpal impaction syndrome).
tus: The ulna does not take part directly in the radiocarpal joint; the articular disc between them (TFCC) separates the ulna from the carpal bones.
Because the centre of the TFCC is avascular, central tears do not heal and are debrided; peripheral tears can be repaired.
models: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

entries.summary: The ellipsoid joint between the lower end of the radius and the articular disc and the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum). The ulna does not take part directly.
facts: Carpal articular surface of the radius and articular disc – scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum
Palmar and dorsal radiocarpal ligaments, palmar ulnocarpal ligament, radial and ulnar collateral ligaments of the wrist
Flexion–extension, radial–ulnar deviation, circumduction; the midcarpal joint adds a large share of the movement
sections: Midcarpal joint

The S-shaped joint between the proximal and distal carpal rows. Most wrist flexion occurs at the radiocarpal joint, while a large part of extension and radial deviation occurs at the midcarpal joint. The dart-throwing motion (from radial extension to ulnar flexion) takes place mainly at the midcarpal joint.
clinical: Scapholunate ligament tear is the commonest cause of wrist instability (Terry Thomas sign: a gap between scaphoid and lunate).
A wrist ganglion is a cystic swelling arising from the joint capsule.
tus: The radiocarpal joint is ellipsoid; flexion–extension and radial–ulnar deviation occur.
Ulnar deviation has a wider range than radial deviation because the radial styloid reaches further down.

entries.summary: The wrist ligaments are thickenings of the capsule: extrinsic ligaments join the radius and ulna to the carpal bones, intrinsic ligaments join the carpal bones to each other. The most important intrinsic ligaments are the scapholunate and lunotriquetral ligaments.
facts: Radioscaphocapitate, radiolunate (long and short), ulnolunate, ulnotriquetral and ulnocapitate ligaments; the palmar ligaments are stronger than the dorsal
Dorsal radiocarpal (radiotriquetral) and dorsal intercarpal ligaments; together they form a 'V' lying on its side
Scapholunate interosseous ligament (its dorsal part is the strongest), lunotriquetral interosseous ligament, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid ligament
Radial collateral ligament of the wrist (radial styloid – scaphoid), ulnar collateral ligament of the wrist (ulnar styloid – triquetrum, pisiform)
Pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments: continuations of the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon
sections: Carpal instability

When the scapholunate ligament tears, the scaphoid rotates into flexion and the lunate into extension (DISI – dorsal intercalated segment instability). If the lunotriquetral ligament tears, the lunate rotates into flexion (VISI). Untreated, a progressive 'SLAC' wrist arthrosis develops.
clinical: In scapholunate tear the AP X-ray shows a gap of more than 3 mm between scaphoid and lunate (Terry Thomas sign) and the 'ring sign' of the scaphoid.
In perilunate dislocation the palmar extrinsic and the intrinsic ligaments tear in sequence (Mayfield stages).
tus: The space of Poirier is an area weak in ligaments around the palmar capitate; perilunate dislocations occur through it.
The pisohamate and pisometacarpal ligaments transmit the pull of flexor carpi ulnaris to the hamate and 5th metacarpal.
models: Radial collateral ligament of wrist joint
Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

entries.summary: The joints between the carpal bones and metacarpals (carpometacarpal), the metacarpals and fingers (metacarpophalangeal) and between the phalanges (interphalangeal).
facts: Saddle joint at the thumb (opposition); 2nd–3rd CMC almost immobile, 4th–5th slightly mobile
Condylar joints; flexion–extension and abduction–adduction; palmar plate and collateral ligaments
Collateral ligaments, palmar ligaments (volar plate), deep transverse metacarpal ligaments
clinical: Skier's thumb: tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint.
In rheumatoid arthritis, ulnar deviation at the MCP joints, swan-neck and boutonnière deformities develop.
tus: The 1st CMC joint is a saddle joint and allows opposition; the 2nd–5th CMC joints are plane joints.
The collateral ligaments of the MCP joints are taut in flexion, so the hand is splinted with the MCP joints flexed.

entries.summary: Saddle-shaped joint between the trapezium and the base of the 1st metacarpal. It makes opposition of the thumb possible and is the basis of the grasping function of the hand.
facts: Synovial saddle joint – biaxial, with a rotational component
Anterior oblique ligament ('beak ligament' – the main stabiliser), dorsoradial ligament, intermetacarpal ligament; lax capsule
Thenar muscles (opponens pollicis, abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis), abductor pollicis longus
clinical: Osteoarthritis at the base of the thumb (rhizarthrosis) is common, especially in postmenopausal women; grasping and turning a key are painful.

In a Bennett fracture the medial fragment of the base of the 1st metacarpal stays in place, held by the anterior oblique ligament, while the main fragment is pulled laterally and proximally by abductor pollicis longus.
tus: The thumb CMC joint is the classic example of a saddle joint (the other is the sternoclavicular joint).
Opposition is produced mainly by opponens pollicis (median nerve).

entries.summary: The metacarpophalangeal (MCP) and interphalangeal (PIP, DIP) joints are supported by collateral ligaments and by the thick fibrocartilaginous volar plate on the palmar side. The deep transverse metacarpal ligaments join the metacarpal heads together.
facts: Ellipsoid (condyloid) joint: flexion-extension, abduction-adduction; the collateral ligaments tighten in flexion (cam effect)
Hinge joints: only flexion-extension; the collateral ligaments are partly tight in every position
Thick fibrocartilaginous plate on the palmar side of the joint; prevents hyperextension
Joins the volar plates of the 2nd–5th metacarpal heads; absent at the thumb
sections: Safe splinting position

When the hand has to be immobilised for long, the MCP joints are held in flexion and the IP joints in extension. In this position the collateral ligaments stay taut, so they do not shorten and cause permanent stiffness.
clinical: Skier's thumb (gamekeeper's thumb) is a tear of the ulnar collateral ligament of the thumb MCP joint; if the ligament end lies on top of the adductor aponeurosis (Stener lesion), surgery is needed.
In hyperextension injuries of the PIP joint the volar plate avulses; untreated, a swan-neck deformity can develop.
tus: 'Safe position' for immobilising the hand: wrist slightly extended, MCPs flexed 70–90°, IPs fully extended.
In a Stener lesion the adductor pollicis aponeurosis comes between the torn ulnar collateral ligament and its insertion.
models: Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints

entries.summary: The joint between the ear-shaped (auricular) surfaces of the sacrum and the hip bone, held by very strong ligaments. It transfers the weight of the trunk to the lower limbs.
facts: Synovial in front, syndesmosis behind (mixed joint); very little movement
Anterior, interosseous (strongest) and posterior sacroiliac ligaments; accessory ligaments: sacrotuberous, sacrospinous, iliolumbar
Very limited gliding and rotation (nutation–counternutation); loosens under hormonal influence in pregnancy
Anterior sacroiliac ligament (thin), interosseous (the strongest – between the two bones), posterior; also the iliolumbar, sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments
clinical: Sacroiliitis is an early sign of seronegative spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis.
It is an often overlooked cause of low back and hip pain.
tus: The front of the sacroiliac joint is synovial, the back a syndesmosis.
Sacroiliitis is an early, characteristic finding of ankylosing spondylitis.
The upper part of the sacroiliac joint is fibrous (syndesmosis), the lower anterior part synovial; it may become fibrous with age.

entries.summary: The joint where the two pubic bones meet in the midline, joined by a fibrocartilaginous disc (interpubic disc).
facts: Superior pubic ligament, inferior (arcuate) pubic ligament
Very limited; widens slightly during childbirth
sections: Structure

Between the hyaline cartilage-covered surfaces of the two pubic bones lies the fibrocartilaginous interpubic disc. The superior pubic ligament above and the inferior (arcuate) pubic ligament below reinforce the joint. It loosens in pregnancy under the influence of relaxin.
clinical: Separation of the symphysis (diastasis) in pregnancy can make walking painful.
Osteitis pubis causes groin pain in athletes.
tus: In pregnancy the symphysis can widen by a few millimetres under the influence of relaxin.
The upper border of the symphysis is the front boundary of the pelvic inlet; the empty bladder lies behind it.

entries.summary: Strong ligaments between the sacrum and the hip bone that turn the sciatic notches into foramina, and the membrane that closes the obturator foramen.
facts: From the edge of the sacrum and coccyx to the ischial tuberosity
From the edge of the sacrum and coccyx to the ischial spine
Greater sciatic foramen (piriformis, gluteal vessels and nerves, sciatic nerve) and lesser sciatic foramen (obturator internus tendon, pudendal nerve)
Closes the obturator foramen, leaving the obturator canal above
From the L5 transverse process to the iliac crest
clinical: A pudendal nerve block (in labour) is given just beside the ischial spine, around the sacrospinous ligament.
tus: The sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments stop the sacrum tipping forwards (nutation).
The iliolumbar ligament binds the L5 transverse process to the iliac crest and limits forward slip of L5.

entries.summary: The ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone. Thanks to its deep socket and strong ligaments it is far more stable than the shoulder.
facts: Head of femur – lunate surface of the acetabulum; the acetabular labrum and transverse acetabular ligament deepen the socket
Iliofemoral ligament (Y ligament – the strongest ligament in the body, prevents hyperextension), pubofemoral ligament, ischiofemoral ligament, ligament of the head of the femur, zona orbicularis
Flexion (~120°), extension (~20°), abduction, adduction, internal and external rotation
Medial (main) and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, obturator artery (artery of the ligament of the head)
Branches of the femoral, obturator and sciatic nerves – hip pain may be referred to the knee
sections: Capsule and femoral neck

In front the capsule reaches the intertrochanteric line and encloses the whole femoral neck; behind it covers only the medial 2/3 of the neck. Femoral neck fractures in front are therefore entirely intracapsular. The retinacular arteries supplying the femoral head run beneath the capsular fibres reflected onto the neck.
clinical: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened in newborns with the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres.
Posterior hip dislocation (e.g. knee striking the dashboard) can injure the sciatic nerve; the leg is short, flexed, adducted and internally rotated.
Advanced hip osteoarthritis needs a total hip replacement; hip pain may be felt in the groin and knee.
tus: The hip is most stable in extension, abduction and internal rotation (ligaments taut).
Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened in newborns with the Ortolani and Barlow manoeuvres.

entries.tr: Ligaments and labrum of the hip joint
entries.summary: Three strong ligaments (iliofemoral, pubofemoral, ischiofemoral) wrap the hip capsule spirally from outside; on standing they 'screw' tight and press the femoral head into the acetabulum. Inside are the labrum, the transverse acetabular ligament and the ligament of the head of the femur.
facts: From the anterior inferior iliac spine and acetabular rim to the intertrochanteric line; shaped like an inverted Y (Bigelow's ligament); the strongest ligament of the body – prevents hyperextension and stops the pelvis tipping backwards when standing
From the superior pubic ramus to the inferior anterior capsule; prevents excessive abduction
From the ischium spirally to the back of the capsule; limits excessive internal rotation and extension
Deep circular capsular fibres encircling the femoral neck; make dislocation of the femoral head harder
Acetabular labrum (deepens the socket), transverse acetabular ligament (bridges the acetabular notch), ligament of the head of the femur (to the fovea capitis)
clinical: Femoroacetabular impingement (FAI) and labral tears are important causes of groin pain in young adults.
The iliofemoral ligament is used as a fulcrum in reducing a dislocated hip; because it stays intact, the leg lies in a typical position in a dislocation.
tus: The iliofemoral ligament (Bigelow's Y ligament) is the strongest ligament of the body and prevents hyperextension of the hip.
The hip ligaments tighten in extension and bring the joint into its most stable (close-packed) position; they slacken in flexion.

entries.summary: The largest and most complex joint in the body. It consists of the joints between the femoral and tibial condyles (tibiofemoral) and between the patella and femur (patellofemoral); its stability depends largely on ligaments and muscles.
facts: Medial meniscus (C-shaped, attached to the medial collateral ligament) and lateral meniscus (O-shaped, more mobile); anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments; infrapatellar fat pad (Hoffa's fat pad)
Tibial (medial) collateral ligament, fibular (lateral) collateral ligament, patellar ligament, oblique and arcuate popliteal ligaments
Flexion (~140°), extension; limited rotation when the knee is bent; locking in full extension as the femur rotates medially (screw-home mechanism)
Suprapatellar bursa (communicates with the joint cavity), prepatellar, infrapatellar, anserine bursae
sections: Cruciate ligaments
The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) stops the tibia sliding forwards on the femur, the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL) stops it sliding backwards. They are named after their tibial attachments.
clinical: 'Unhappy triad' (O'Donoghue): combined injury of the medial collateral ligament, ACL and medial meniscus from a blow to the outer side of the knee.
In an ACL tear the anterior drawer and Lachman tests are positive.
Meniscal tears cause joint-line tenderness, locking and a positive McMurray test.
A Baker's (popliteal) cyst behind the knee is common.
tus: The knee has three compartments: medial and lateral femorotibial and patellofemoral.
The suprapatellar bursa communicates with the joint cavity; a knee effusion is felt here (patellar tap).

entries.summary: Two fibrocartilaginous rings, triangular in section, between the femoral and tibial condyles. They improve the fit of the articular surfaces and spread the load.
facts: C-shaped and wide; attached to the tibial collateral ligament, so less mobile and more often torn
Roughly O-shaped, smaller and more mobile; connected to popliteus
Meniscotibial ligaments, transverse ligament of the knee, meniscofemoral ligaments
Only the outer third (red zone) is vascularised; the inner part heals poorly
sections: Function

The menisci carry about half the load passing through the knee, make the articular surfaces congruent, absorb shock and help spread the synovial fluid. Removing a meniscus (meniscectomy) leads to early osteoarthritis, so repair is preferred whenever possible.
clinical: A sudden twist of the bent, weight-bearing knee tears a meniscus; a bucket-handle tear can lock the knee.
tus: The outer third of the menisci is vascularised (red zone) and can be repaired; the inner two thirds are avascular.
Bucket-handle tears cause locking of the joint.

entries.summary: Two strong ligaments that cross each other inside the knee joint (but outside the synovial membrane): the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) and the posterior cruciate ligament (PCL).
facts: From the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the inner surface of the lateral femoral condyle; prevents forward slide of the tibia and hyperextension
From the posterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the outer surface of the medial femoral condyle; prevents backward slide of the tibia; the stronger of the two
sections: Position

The cruciate ligaments lie inside the joint capsule but outside the synovial membrane (intracapsular, extrasynovial). The ACL runs from anteromedial to posterolateral, the PCL from anterolateral to posteromedial; they cross each other in an X.
clinical: ACL tears occur in athletes during sudden changes of direction and landings; a 'pop' and rapid swelling (haemarthrosis) are typical.
PCL tears occur in dashboard injuries (bent knee striking the dashboard); the posterior drawer test is positive.
tus: The ACL runs from the anterior intercondylar area of the tibia to the inner surface of the lateral femoral condyle, the PCL from the posterior intercondylar area to the outer surface of the medial condyle.
The cruciate ligaments lie inside the joint capsule but outside the synovial membrane (intracapsular, extrasynovial).

entries.summary: Ligaments supporting the medial and lateral sides of the knee; they prevent the knee opening sideways (valgus/varus).
facts: Medial femoral epicondyle – medial surface of the tibia; broad and flat, attached to the medial meniscus; resists valgus force
Lateral femoral epicondyle – head of the fibula; a round cord, separate from the meniscus; resists varus force
Both are taut in full extension
sections: Differences

The medial collateral ligament is fused with the capsule and the medial meniscus, so the medial meniscus may be involved in its injuries. The lateral collateral ligament is separate from the capsule and the lateral meniscus; the popliteus tendon passes between them.
clinical: Blows to the outer side of the knee strain the medial collateral ligament; it is assessed with the valgus stress test.
tus: The medial collateral ligament is broad and flat and attaches to the medial meniscus; the lateral one is a round cord that does not attach to the meniscus.
The collateral ligaments are taut in extension and lax in flexion.
models: Superficial part of tibial collateral ligament
Deep part of tibial collateral ligament

entries.tr: Posterior and posterolateral ligaments of the knee
entries.en: Posterior and posterolateral ligaments of knee
entries.summary: The back of the knee capsule is reinforced by the oblique and arcuate popliteal ligaments. Together with the lateral collateral ligament, the popliteofibular ligament and the popliteus tendon they form the 'posterolateral corner', which provides varus and external rotation stability of the knee.
facts: An expansion of the semimembranosus tendon; runs upwards and laterally; reinforces the back of the capsule and limits hyperextension
Arises from the head of the fibula and arches over the popliteus tendon to blend with the capsule
From the popliteus tendon to the head of the fibula; the most important static stabiliser of the posterolateral corner
Lateral collateral ligament, popliteus tendon, popliteofibular ligament, arcuate popliteal ligament, capsule
Attach the anterior and posterior horns of the menisci to the tibia (coronary ligaments)
clinical: Posterolateral corner injuries usually accompany cruciate ligament injuries; if missed, ligament reconstructions fail. External rotation is increased on the dial test.
In posterolateral corner injuries the common fibular nerve, which winds around the head of the fibula, may also be damaged.
tus: The oblique popliteal ligament is an expansion of the semimembranosus tendon.
On the dial test, increased external rotation at 30° only suggests a posterolateral corner injury; increased rotation at both 30° and 90° suggests a combined posterolateral corner and PCL injury.

entries.summary: The upper synovial joint between tibia and fibula, the syndesmosis below and the interosseous membrane of the leg between their shafts.
facts: Tibiofibular joint: synovial plane joint (head of fibula – lateral tibial condyle)
Tibiofibular syndesmosis: anterior and posterior tibiofibular ligaments; it stabilises the ankle mortise
Gives attachment to the leg muscles and separates the anterior and posterior compartments
clinical: A high ankle sprain is a tear of the syndesmotic ligaments and takes longer to heal.
tus: The proximal tibiofibular joint is a synovial plane joint, the distal one a syndesmosis.
In a high ankle sprain (syndesmosis injury) the external rotation test is positive.
The capsule of the superior tibiofibular joint sometimes communicates with the knee joint cavity.

entries.summary: The fibrous joint binding the lower ends of the tibia and fibula together. It maintains the width of the ankle mortise; in dorsiflexion the talus spreads this mortise slightly.
facts: Anterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, posterior inferior tibiofibular ligament, transverse tibiofibular ligament (deep part of the posterior ligament), interosseous ligament (lower continuation of the interosseous membrane)
Grips the mortise tightly; because the talus is wider in front, the fibula moves slightly outwards and upwards in dorsiflexion
clinical: A high ankle sprain occurs with external rotation; the syndesmotic ligaments tear and healing takes much longer than a lateral ligament sprain. The squeeze test is positive.
In a Maisonneuve fracture the syndesmosis and interosseous membrane tear and the upper fibula breaks; in ankle injuries the area below the knee must also be examined.
tus: Maisonneuve fracture: fracture of the medial malleolus or tear of the deltoid ligament + syndesmotic tear + proximal fibular fracture.
Widening caused by syndesmotic injury is assessed on X-ray by measuring the tibiofibular clear space.

entries.summary: The hinge joint between the mortise formed by the lower ends of the tibia and fibula and the trochlea of the talus.
facts: Lower surface of the tibia and medial malleolus, lateral malleolus – trochlea of the talus
Medial collateral (deltoid) ligament: tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts – very strong
Anterior talofibular ligament (the most often torn), calcaneofibular ligament, posterior talofibular ligament
Dorsiflexion (~20°) and plantar flexion (~50°); inversion–eversion occur at the subtalar joint
Most stable in dorsiflexion because the trochlea is wider in front; prone to sprains in plantar flexion
sections: Mortise

The lower surface of the tibia and the two malleoli form a fork (mortise) gripping the talus on three sides. The lateral malleolus reaches lower and lies further back than the medial; eversion is therefore more limited than inversion. Bimalleolar and trimalleolar fractures disrupt the integrity of the mortise.
clinical: Most ankle sprains occur in plantar flexion + inversion, and the anterior talofibular ligament tears first.
The Ottawa rules decide whether an X-ray is needed after an ankle injury.
Pott's fracture: in an eversion injury, a deltoid ligament tear or medial malleolus fracture combined with a fibular fracture.
tus: The deltoid ligament has four parts (tibionavicular, tibiocalcaneal, anterior and posterior tibiotalar) and limits eversion.
The Ottawa rules determine the need for X-rays after ankle trauma.

entries.summary: Three separate ligaments running from the lateral malleolus to the talus and calcaneus. Because they are much weaker than the deltoid ligament on the medial side, they are the structures most often injured in ankle sprains.
facts: Anterior border of the lateral malleolus – neck of the talus; flat and the weakest ligament; tight in plantar flexion
Tip of the lateral malleolus – lateral surface of the calcaneus; cord-like; passes deep to the fibular tendons; supports both the ankle and the subtalar joint
Malleolar fossa of the lateral malleolus – posterior process of the talus; the strongest lateral ligament and the most rarely torn
First the anterior talofibular, then the calcaneofibular, last the posterior talofibular ligament tears
clinical: The anterior drawer test assesses the anterior talofibular ligament, the talar tilt (inversion stress) test the calcaneofibular ligament.
Repeated sprains can lead to chronic lateral instability; surgical repair (Broström) may be performed.
tus: 85% of ankle sprains are inversion injuries and the anterior talofibular ligament tears first.
The calcaneofibular ligament is the only lateral ligament that contributes to both the ankle and the subtalar joint.

entries.tr: Deltoid ligament (medial ligament of the ankle)
entries.summary: A very strong, triangular ligament fanning out from the medial malleolus to the navicular, calcaneus and talus. It prevents the ankle from opening with eversion and external rotation.
facts: Tibionavicular part (to the navicular tuberosity and spring ligament), tibiocalcaneal part (to the sustentaculum tali)
Anterior and posterior tibiotalar parts (to the medial surface of the talus); the deep part is the main stabiliser preventing lateral shift of the talus
Limits eversion, supports the medial side of the ankle and the medial arch
So strong that in forced eversion the medial malleolus may break off (avulsion) before the ligament tears
clinical: If the deltoid ligament tears in an eversion-external rotation injury, the talus shifts laterally in the mortise; untreated, ankle arthrosis develops.
In adult acquired flatfoot, failure of tibialis posterior is accompanied by laxity of the deltoid and spring ligaments.
tus: The deep tibiotalar part of the deltoid ligament is the most important structure preventing lateral shift of the talus.
In eversion injuries the medial malleolus may fracture instead of the deltoid ligament tearing (Pott fracture mechanism).

entries.summary: The joints between the tarsal bones (subtalar, talocalcaneonavicular, calcaneocuboid), the tarsometatarsal, metatarsophalangeal and interphalangeal joints, and the ligaments supporting the arches of the foot.
facts: Talus – calcaneus; most inversion and eversion occur here
Tarsal bones and metatarsal bases; the base of the 2nd metatarsal is the keystone
Plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament – supports the head of the talus, long plantar ligament, plantar calcaneocuboid ligament, plantar aponeurosis
Medial and lateral longitudinal arches, transverse arch
clinical: Lisfranc injuries can be missed and lead to chronic pain and deformity.
Failure of the spring ligament contributes to flat foot (pes planus).
Hallux rigidus is osteoarthritis of the 1st metatarsophalangeal joint; restricted dorsiflexion causes pain in the push-off phase.
tus: Chopart (transverse tarsal) joint: talonavicular + calcaneocuboid; Lisfranc joint: the tarsometatarsal joints.
The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament supports the head of the talus; its failure leads to flat foot.

entries.summary: The joint between the inferior surface of the talus and the upper surface of the calcaneus. Most of the movements raising the inner and outer borders of the foot (inversion and eversion) take place here; it allows walking on uneven ground.
facts: Anatomical subtalar joint: posterior calcaneal facet of the talus – posterior talar facet of the calcaneus. The clinical (functional) subtalar joint also includes the talocalcaneonavicular joint with the anterior and middle facets
Synovial plane joint (functionally a uniaxial joint with an oblique axis)
Interosseous talocalcaneal ligament (in the sinus tarsi, the strongest), lateral, medial, anterior and posterior talocalcaneal ligaments; the calcaneofibular ligament also supports it
A tunnel between talus and calcaneus opening laterally; contains the interosseous ligament and fat
clinical: Calcaneal fractures usually involve the subtalar articular surface and can lead to permanent subtalar arthrosis.
Sinus tarsi syndrome causes persistent pain on the lateral side of the foot after ankle sprains.
tus: Inversion and eversion occur mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints, not at the ankle joint.
Talocalcaneal coalition is the commonest coalition of the talocalcaneonavicular joint and shows the 'C sign'.

entries.summary: S-shaped joint line formed by the talonavicular and calcaneocuboid joints, between the hindfoot and the midfoot. Together with the subtalar joint it takes part in inversion-eversion.
facts: Talocalcaneonavicular joint (head of talus – navicular and spring ligament) and calcaneocuboid joint

Bifurcate ligament (Y ligament: calcaneonavicular and calcaneocuboid parts), talonavicular ligament, plantar calcaneonavicular ligament (spring ligament), plantar calcaneocuboid ligament (short plantar ligament), long plantar ligament
One of the amputation levels of the foot (Chopart amputation)
clinical: Chopart injuries can be missed as ankle sprains; a sprain of the bifurcate ligament causes pain on the lateral side of the foot, in front of the sinus tarsi.
After Chopart amputation the stump may drop into equinus (plantar flexion) through the unbalanced pull of the Achilles tendon.
tus: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament supports the head of the talus from below and is the key ligament of the medial arch.
The two limbs of the bifurcate ligament run from the calcaneus to the navicular and the cuboid.

entries.summary: The joints between the three cuneiforms and the cuboid and the bases of the five metatarsals. The locking of the 2nd metatarsal base between the cuneiforms and the Lisfranc ligament give this joint its stability.
facts: Synovial plane joints; three separate synovial cavities (medial, middle, lateral columns)
Medial cuneiform – 1st metatarsal; intermediate and lateral cuneiforms – 2nd and 3rd metatarsals; cuboid – 4th and 5th metatarsals
Strong interosseous ligament from the medial cuneiform to the base of the 2nd metatarsal; there is no ligament between the bases of the 1st and 2nd metatarsals
Dorsal and plantar tarsometatarsal ligaments (the plantar ones are stronger), cuneometatarsal interosseous ligaments
clinical: A Lisfranc injury (tarsometatarsal fracture-dislocation) occurs with a fall onto a plantar-flexed foot or crushing of the foot from behind; plantar bruising is typical and about 20% are missed at first presentation.
The Lisfranc line is one of the levels used for foot amputations.
tus: Bruising of the sole (plantar ecchymosis) should suggest a Lisfranc injury.
On X-ray the medial border of the 2nd metatarsal should line up with the medial border of the intermediate cuneiform; a shift indicates a Lisfranc injury.

entries.summary: The bones of the foot do not form a flat platform but two longitudinal arches and one transverse arch. The arches distribute load between the heel and the metatarsal heads and act as shock absorber and lever in walking; they are maintained by the shape of the bones, by ligaments and by muscles.
facts: Calcaneus, talus, navicular, three cuneiforms and 1st–3rd metatarsals; high and flexible; its keystone is the head of the talus
Calcaneus, cuboid, 4th–5th metatarsals; low, close to the ground; its keystone is the cuboid
Cuneiforms, cuboid and metatarsal bases; most marked in the forefoot
Plantar aponeurosis (the most important – 'windlass' mechanism), long plantar ligament, plantar calcaneocuboid ligament, plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament
Tibialis posterior, fibularis longus, tibialis anterior, flexor hallucis longus, intrinsic muscles of the sole
sections: Windlass mechanism

In the push-off phase of walking, when the big toe dorsiflexes, the plantar aponeurosis winds around the metatarsal heads and tightens; it pulls the heel forwards, raises the medial arch and turns the foot into a rigid lever.
clinical: Flatfoot (pes planus) is collapse of the medial arch; in adults the commonest cause is failure of the tibialis posterior tendon.
Pes cavus (high arch) may be seen in neuromuscular diseases such as Charcot–Marie–Tooth.
Plantar fasciitis is degeneration of the plantar aponeurosis at its attachment to the calcaneus; heel pain with the first steps in the morning is typical.
tus: The keystone of the medial longitudinal arch is the head of the talus, that of the lateral arch the cuboid; the spring ligament (plantar calcaneonavicular) supports the head of the talus from below.
The tendons of fibularis longus and tibialis anterior form a 'stirrup' under the foot that supports the transverse and medial arches.
